docs.title: Avora — Avora Version Control System
docs.text: Avora is a version-control system purpose-built for legal contracts. It tracks changes to .docx documents through a Git-like workflow — branches, commits, logs, diffs, and merges — without requiring users to leave their word processor.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The project is split into two packages:

  • avora — the command-line client used to initialize repositories, commit changes, branch, merge, and push/pull from a remote host.
  • remote_avora — a self-hosted FastAPI server that stores repositories and serves them over HTTP so multiple users can clone, push, and pull.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Initialize a new contract repository from a .docx file (avora init)
  • Commit changes with descriptive messages
  • Branch, merge, and switch between branches
  • View commit history (avora log) and diffs (avora diff)
  • Revert a document to any past commit
  • Reset uncommitted changes
  • Push and pull repositories to/from a self-hosted remote server
  • Publish a local repository for others to clone

docs.title: avora
docs.text:
The local command-line tool. Install from PyPI with:

pip install avora

Once installed, the avora command is available. Run avora help for the full list of commands.

Commands: init, commit, branch, merge, switch, clone, push, pull, publish, log, diff, open, revert, reset, status, config, help

docs.title: remote_avora
docs.text:
The self-hosted server. Install from PyPI with:

pip install remote-avora

Start a server with:

remote-avora serve

The server exposes endpoints for cloning, pushing, pulling, and publishing repositories. By default it serves from the current directory and stores repositories under repos/.

docs.title: Initialize a local repository
docs.text:
avora init contract.docx
cd contract

docs.title: Make and commit changes
docs.text: avora commit -m "Updated liability section"

docs.title: Host a remote server
docs.text: remote-avora serve

docs.title: Clone from a remote
docs.text: avora clone http://<server-ip>/repos/my-repo/clone

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
Each initialized Avora repository contains a .avora/ directory with:

  • metadata.json — branch information, current branch, and commit order
  • objects/docx/ — stored document versions keyed by commit identifier
  • objects/html/ — HTML versions for diffing
  • objects/view_html/ — standalone HTML pages for viewing commits

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Full documentation is available at Avora Documentation.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• avora — depends on mammoth, requests, and beautifulsoup4
  • remote_avora — depends on fastapi[standard]

docs.title: You are a senior software engineer performing a thorough pull request review.
Objective
docs.text:
Analyze this PR as if it will be merged into a production codebase. Determine whether the changes introduced or materially affected by this PR are correct, secure, reliable, maintainable, performant, and adequately tested.

Review the PR in the context of the relevant surrounding codebase, including callers, dependencies, interfaces, configuration, related implementations, and existing tests where necessary.

Do not limit the review to the changed lines when understanding the impact of a change requires examining other code.

docs.title: 1. Correctness
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Logic bugs
  • Incorrect assumptions
  • Incorrect state transitions
  • Edge cases
  • Race conditions
  • Incorrect handling of return values or state
  • Error handling problems
  • Unexpected behavior
  • Breaking changes to existing behavior or interfaces

docs.title: 2. Security
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Authentication or authorization flaws
  • Missing or inadequate input validation
  • Injection vulnerabilities
  • Data exposure
  • Unsafe handling of user-controlled data
  • Insecure defaults
  • Trust-boundary violations
  • Path traversal or unsafe file operations
  • Dependency or configuration risks
  • Sensitive information exposed through logs, errors, or responses

docs.title: 3. Code quality and maintainability
docs.text:
Look for problems that materially affect the ability to safely maintain or extend the code, including:

  • Poor architectural decisions
  • Unnecessary complexity
  • Hard-to-maintain implementations
  • Significant duplication
  • Violations of important design principles
  • Missing abstractions when an abstraction is clearly required
  • Tight coupling that creates meaningful correctness or maintenance risks

Do not report purely subjective preferences.

docs.title: 4. Performance and scalability
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Inefficient algorithms
  • Unnecessary database, filesystem, or API calls
  • Excessive memory usage
  • Resource leaks
  • Unbounded operations
  • Blocking operations in inappropriate contexts
  • Performance problems that become significant at realistic production scale

Only report performance concerns when there is a meaningful or plausible production impact.

docs.title: 5. Reliability
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Missing or inadequate error handling
  • Incorrect exception handling
  • Failures that can leave the system in an invalid or inconsistent state
  • Partial updates
  • Missing cleanup
  • Retry or recovery problems
  • Transactionality issues
  • Problems with logging, monitoring, or operational recovery

docs.title: 6. Testing
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Missing tests for important new behavior
  • Incorrect or ineffective tests
  • Missing regression tests for bugs fixed by the PR
  • Untested error paths
  • Untested security-sensitive behavior
  • Untested edge cases
  • Tests that could pass while the implementation is incorrect

Do not report the absence of tests unless the missing coverage creates a meaningful regression risk.

docs.title: Review rules
docs.text:
• Only report issues that are meaningful, actionable, and relevant to this PR.
  • Prioritize severity over quantity.
  • Do not report formatting, naming, or minor style differences unless they cause a real functional, security, reliability, maintainability, or performance problem.
  • Do not praise the code.
  • Do not summarize the PR unless necessary to explain a finding.
  • Do not report speculative issues as confirmed defects.
  • If an issue depends on information that cannot be verified from the available codebase, clearly identify the uncertainty.

  • Distinguish between:

  • Confirmed defects — the available code demonstrates that the problem exists.

  • Potential risks — the problem is plausible but requires additional verification.
  • Do not report pre-existing problems unless the PR introduces them, exposes them, or materially worsens them.
  • Consider interactions between multiple changes, not just individual lines.
  • Prefer concrete evidence from the code over assumptions about intended behavior.
  • Avoid duplicate findings that describe the same underlying problem.
  • Prioritize findings that could cause incorrect behavior, security incidents, data loss, production outages, or significant maintenance problems.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Use only these severity levels:

  • Critical — Immediate, severe production impact; for example, catastrophic security vulnerabilities, data loss, system-wide failure, or a defect that makes the system fundamentally unsafe to deploy.
  • High — Serious production impact that should block merging; for example, significant security vulnerabilities, major correctness bugs, or likely data corruption.
  • Medium — Meaningful defect or risk that should generally be fixed before or shortly after merging.
  • Low — Minor issue with limited impact.

Do not report Low-severity issues.

When assigning severity, consider both the likelihood of occurrence and the potential impact.

docs.title: Required format for every finding
docs.text: For every issue, provide:

docs.title: [Severity] Short issue title
docs.text:
• File: path/to/file
  • Line: <line number or range>
  • Problem: Clearly explain what is wrong.
  • Why it matters: Explain the concrete production impact, including relevant failure scenarios.
  • Recommended fix: Give a specific, actionable remediation.

For multi-line issues, identify the smallest relevant line range.

docs.title: Final assessment
docs.text: At the end of the review, provide:

docs.title: Overall PR quality: X/10
docs.text: Rate the PR based on its production readiness, not merely code quality.

docs.title: Most important risks
docs.text: Briefly identify the most significant risks found, ordered by severity.

docs.title: Merge decision
docs.text:
Choose exactly one:

  • Safe to merge
  • Not safe to merge

If the PR is not safe to merge, identify the issue(s) that must be resolved before merging.

Do not mark a PR unsafe to merge solely because of optional improvements or minor test coverage gaps.

docs.title: avora — Avora Version Control System
docs.text: avora is the command-line client for Avora, a version-control system purpose-built for legal contracts. It tracks changes to .docx documents through a Git-like workflow — branches, commits, logs, diffs, and merges — without requiring users to leave their word processor.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Initialize a new contract repository from a .docx file
  • Commit changes with descriptive messages
  • Branch, merge, and switch between branches
  • View commit history and diffs
  • Revert a document to any past commit
  • Reset uncommitted changes
  • Push and pull repositories to/from a self-hosted remote server
  • Publish a local repository for others to clone

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
The avora command provides 17 subcommands covering the full version-control lifecycle:

init, commit, branch, merge, switch, clone, push, pull, publish, log, diff, open, revert, reset, status, config, help

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• mammoth — converts .docx to HTML for diffing
  • requests — HTTP client for remote operations
  • beautifulsoup4 — parses HTML diff output

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Installation — how to install avora and set up your environment
  • Usage — command reference, examples, and workflows
  • Avora Documentation — full project documentation

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or later
  • A .docx file (Microsoft Word or compatible) for initializing repositories

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
pip install avora

This installs the avora command-line tool and its dependencies.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
avora help

This prints the list of available commands and flags.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
avora installs the following Python packages automatically:

Package Purpose mammoth Converts .docx to HTML for diffing requests HTTP client for remote operations (push, pull, clone, publish) beautifulsoup4 Parses HTML diff output

docs.title: Development Installation
docs.text:
To install from source for development:

git clone https://github.com/Avora-Docx/Avora-Docx
cd legal-contract-version-control
pip install -e packages/avora

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
To upgrade to the latest version:

pip install --upgrade avora

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text: pip uninstall avora

docs.title: Command Reference
docs.text: All commands are run within an Avora repository directory (the directory created by avora init).

docs.title: avora init <document_path>
docs.text:
Initialize a new Avora repository from a .docx file. The original document is copied into the repository and the first commit is created automatically with the message "Initial commit (This is a default commit message for the initial version)". You will be prompted for your name and email.

avora init contract.docx
cd contract

docs.title: avora commit -m <message>
docs.text:
Commit uncommitted changes to the current branch with a descriptive message.

avora commit -m "Updated liability section"

docs.title: avora branch <subcommand> [branch_name]
docs.text:
Manage branches. Three subcommands:

# Create a new branch from the current branch
avora branch create feature-x

# Delete an existing branch (cannot delete the current branch or 'main')
avora branch delete feature-x

# List all branches (current branch is marked with *)
avora branch list

docs.title: avora switch <branch_name>
docs.text:
Switch the working document to a different branch.

avora switch feature-x

docs.title: avora merge <branch_name>
docs.text:
Merge the specified branch into the current branch. Cannot merge a branch into itself.

avora merge feature-x

docs.title: avora log
docs.text:
Print the commit history of the current branch, including commit identifier, author, date, and message for each commit.

avora log

docs.title: avora diff <commit_identifier>
docs.text:
Show differences between the current document and a past commit. The diff is rendered as HTML and written to diff.html in the repository root. Accepts a 10-character short identifier or a full 64-character hash.

avora diff a1b2c3d4e5

docs.title: avora open <commit_identifier>
docs.text:
Open a past commit as a separate .docx file. The original commit is not modified; a new file is created for editing.

avora open a1b2c3d4e5

docs.title: avora revert <commit_identifier>
docs.text:
Revert the current document to the specified commit, creating a new commit with the reverted content.

avora revert a1b2c3d4e5

docs.title: avora reset
docs.text:
Delete all uncommitted changes and restore the document to the latest commit.

avora reset

docs.title: avora status
docs.text:
Check the status of the current document for uncommitted changes.

avora status

docs.title: avora config <key> <value>
docs.text:
Configure repository settings. Accepted keys:

Key Description remote The base URL of the remote Avora server (stored per-repository) name The author name for commits (stored globally in ~/.config/avora/config.json) email The author email for commits (stored globally in ~/.config/avora/config.json) 
avora config name "Jane Doe"
avora config email "jane@example.com"
avora config remote "http://192.168.1.10"

The remote URL must use http or https and will be automatically appended with /repos/<repository-name>/. The name and email values are stored globally and shared across all repositories.

docs.title: avora clone <url>
docs.text:
Clone a hosted Avora repository. The URL must end with /clone (e.g., http://host:8000/repos/<repository-name>/clone).

avora clone http://192.168.1.10/repos/my-repo/clone

docs.title: avora push
docs.text:
Push local changes to the configured remote repository. Fails if the remote has commits the local repository is missing.

avora push

docs.title: avora pull
docs.text:
Pull changes from the configured remote repository and merge them into the local repository. Fails if there are uncommitted changes in the working tree.

avora pull

docs.title: avora publish
docs.text:
Publish a local repository to the configured remote server so others can clone it.

avora publish

docs.title: avora help
docs.text:
Print the list of available commands and flags.

avora help

docs.title: Flags
docs.text: Flag Description -d, --debug Run in debug mode; does not catch exceptions or AvoraException

docs.title: Commit Identifiers
docs.text:
Commit identifiers are SHA-256 hashes derived from the program start timestamp, commit message, and author. Two forms are accepted:

  • Short — the first 10 characters, sufficient for most commands
  • Full — the complete 64-character hash, required when short identifiers are ambiguous

Note: The timestamp component is the program start time (when the avora command was invoked), not the individual commit time.

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
Each Avora repository contains a .avora/ directory:

  • metadata.json — branch information, current branch, and commit order
  • objects/docx/ — stored document versions keyed by commit identifier
  • objects/html/ — HTML versions for diffing
  • objects/view_html/ — standalone HTML pages for viewing commits

docs.title: Workflow Example
docs.text:
# Initialize
avora init contract.docx
cd contract

# Configure author
avora config name "Jane Doe"
avora config email "jane@example.com"

# Make edits and commit
avora commit -m "Initial draft"

# Create a revision branch
avora branch create revisions
avora switch revisions

# Make more edits
avora commit -m "Added exhibits"

# Merge back to main
avora switch main
avora merge revisions

# View history
avora log

# Push to remote
avora push

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Expected error (invalid command, missing file, etc.) 2 Unexpected error (also occurs without --debug)

docs.title: Our Pledge
docs.text:
We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

docs.title: Our Standards
docs.text:
Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

  • Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
  • Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
  • Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
  • Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
  • Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

  • The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
  • Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
  • Public or private harassment
  • Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
  • Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

docs.title: Enforcement Responsibilities
docs.text:
Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement by emailing danielaphillion@icloud.com. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

docs.title: Enforcement Guidelines
docs.text: Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

docs.title: 1. Correction
docs.text:
Community Impact: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

Consequence: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

docs.title: 2. Warning
docs.text:
Community Impact: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

Consequence: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

docs.title: 3. Temporary Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

Consequence: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

docs.title: 4. Permanent Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

Consequence: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

docs.title: Attribution
docs.text:
This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.0, available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/0/code_of_conduct.html.

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder.

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq. Translations are available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations.

docs.title: Contributing to Avora
docs.text:
Pre-Alpha. Avora is still in early development and likely has many bugs or missing features. If you discover a bug or would like to suggest a feature, please open an issue with the relevant label. Contributions of all kinds — code, documentation, bug reports, and ideas — are greatly appreciated!

Thank you for your interest in contributing to Avora, a version-control system purpose-built for legal contracts. This guide explains how to set up a development environment, the conventions we follow, and how to submit changes.

docs.title: Code of Conduct
docs.text: By participating in this project, you agree to abide by our Code of Conduct. Please be respectful, welcoming, and constructive in all interactions.

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
Avora is a Python monorepo. Each package is independently buildable and published to PyPI.

legal-contract-version-control/
├── packages/
│   ├── avora/      # `avora` CLI — distributed as the `avora` package
│   │   ├── src/avora/
│   │   ├── tests/
│   │   └── pyproject.toml
│   └── remote_avora/     # `remote-avora` FastAPI server — distributed as `remote-avora`
│       ├── src/remote_avora/
│       ├── tests/
│       └── pyproject.toml
├── docs/                # MkDocs (Material) documentation source
├── mkdocs.yml           # Documentation site config
└── dev_requirements.txt # Shared development/test dependencies
  • avora — the command-line client used to initialize repositories, commit changes, branch, merge, and push/pull from a remote host. Entry point: avora.avora_entrypoint:main.
  • remote_avora — a self-hosted FastAPI server that stores repositories and serves them over HTTP so multiple users can clone, push, and pull. Entry point: remote_avora.remote_avora_entrypoint:main.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or higher. Avora uses modern typing syntax (e.g. PEP 695 generics); older versions will not run. Download from python.org.
  • Git — for version control and submitting changes.
  • A GitHub account — to open issues and submit pull requests.

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository on GitHub, then clone your fork:

bash git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/legal-contract-version-control.git cd legal-contract-version-control

  1. Create and activate a virtual environment (recommended, keeps dependencies isolated):

bash python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate

  1. Install the shared development dependencies (pytest, formatters, and runtime deps for both packages):

bash pip install -r dev_requirements.txt

  1. Install the packages in editable mode so your changes are reflected without reinstalling:

bash pip install -e packages/avora pip install -e packages/remote_avora

docs.title: Running the CLI
docs.text:
With the packages installed (editable or otherwise), the console scripts are available on your PATH:

avora help              # list all avora commands
remote-avora serve      # start the remote server (serves from the current directory)

avora provides 17 subcommands covering the full version-control lifecycle: init, commit, branch, merge, switch, clone, push, pull, publish, log, diff, open, revert, reset, status, config, help.

remote-avora provides serve and help.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Tests use pytest and live alongside each package under packages/<package>/tests/. pytest-asyncio is used for the async FastAPI server tests.

Run the full suite from the repository root:

pytest

Run a single package's tests:

# avora (CLI)
pytest packages/avora/tests

# remote_avora (server)
pytest packages/remote_avora/tests

Run a single test file or test:

pytest packages/avora/tests/test_commit.py
pytest packages/avora/tests/test_commit.py::test_commit_main_raises_if_commit_message_is_empty

Generate a coverage report:

pytest --cov=avora --cov=remote_avora

When working in packages/avora/tests, note that conftest.py imports shared test constants via from test_constants import .... Run tests with that directory on the path (the default pytest invocation from the repo root handles this) if you hit import errors.

docs.title: Code Style & Formatting
docs.text:
Code is formatted with black and isort using the black profile. A CI workflow (.github/workflows/format.yml) automatically runs both on pull requests that touch .py files and commits the formatting back to same-repo branches.

To format locally before pushing:

pip install black isort
isort --profile black .
black .

Keep changes consistent with the surrounding code, use descriptive names, and include docstrings on new functions/classes as the existing code does.

docs.title: Find Something to Do
docs.text:
The easiest way to get started is to browse the Issues tab:

  • Look for issues labeled good first issue if you're new to the project.
  • Check for issues labeled help wanted for tasks we'd love community help with.
  • If you have an idea that isn't already tracked, open a new issue to discuss it before starting work.

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository on GitHub.
  2. Clone your fork locally (see Project Setup).
  3. Create a branch for your work (see Commit Guidelines for naming):

bash git checkout -b feature/my-new-feature

  1. Make your changes, keeping them focused and well-tested.
  2. Format and test your changes (see Code Style & Formatting and Testing).
  3. Commit your changes following the guidelines below.
  4. Push your branch to your fork:

bash git push origin feature/my-new-feature

  1. Open a Pull Request against the main branch of the upstream repository.

docs.title: Commit Guidelines
docs.text:
Avora uses the Conventional Commits format. A commit message template is provided in .git_commit_template — enable it locally with:

git config commit.template .git_commit_template

Format:

<type>(<scope>): <short description>

[optional body: explain WHY the change was made]

[optional footer: e.g. Closes #42]

docs.title: Commit Types
docs.text: Type Purpose feat New feature fix Bug fix refactor Restructure code without changing behavior perf Performance improvement style Formatting only (whitespace, formatting) docs Documentation changes test Add or modify tests chore Maintenance tasks (configs, dependencies) build Build system changes ci CI/CD configuration changes revert Revert a previous commit wip Work in progress debug Debugging changes

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
feat(commit): add diff command for tracked files
fix(config): handle empty config on first read
tests(push): update push tests for new remote layout
docs(readme): document remote_avora setup

Guidelines:

  • Use the imperative mood (Add ..., not Added ...).
  • Keep commits focused — one logical change per commit is easier to review.
  • Reference the related issue where applicable (e.g. Closes #42).

docs.title: Branch Naming
docs.text:
Use a short, descriptive prefix:

Prefix Purpose feature/ New features or enhancements fix/ Bug fixes docs/ Documentation changes test/ Adding or updating tests refactor/ Code changes that don't change behavior

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
• Target the main branch of the upstream repository.
  • Fill out the PR template (docs/pull_request_template.md) and describe what changed and why.
  • Link any related issues (e.g. Closes #42).
  • Ensure your code is formatted (black + isort) and that the test suite passes.
  • Ensure the CLI commands still work as expected for any behavior you touched.
  • Be responsive to review feedback. An automated AI reviewer (.github/workflows/pr-review.yml, prompt in docs/PR_REVIEWER.md) runs on PRs and posts findings; address or discuss them as part of the review.

docs.title: Reporting Bugs & Suggesting Features
docs.text:
Before opening a new issue, please search existing issues to avoid duplicates. Use the provided templates under .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/:

  • Bugs (bug_report.md) — include steps to reproduce, expected vs. actual behavior, your OS + version, and Python version.
  • Features (feature_request.md) — describe the problem you're trying to solve and propose a solution if you have one.

Apply the appropriate label (bug or enhancement) when creating the issue.

docs.title: Need Help?
docs.text:
If you get stuck or have questions, feel free to open an issue or reach out. We're happy to help you get your contribution merged!

Thank you for helping make Avora better!

docs.title: remote_avora — Self-Hosted Avora Server
docs.text: remote_avora is a self-hosted FastAPI server that stores Avora repositories and serves them over HTTP. It enables multiple users to clone, push, pull, and publish contract repositories, turning the local avora CLI into a collaborative version-control system.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Clone — download a repository as a zip archive
  • Push — upload new objects to a repository incrementally
  • Pull — download missing objects and metadata from a remote
  • Publish — upload a full repository for others to clone
  • Zip-slip protection — all archive extractions are path-safe
  • Size limits — per-file, total upload, and file count limits enforced

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
The remote-avora command provides 2 subcommands:

serve, help

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: • fastapi[standard] — web framework including Uvicorn server

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Installation — how to install remote-avora and start a server
  • Usage — endpoints, configuration, and operational details
  • Avora Documentation — full project documentation

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or later
  • Sufficient disk space to store repositories (default: ./repos/ in the working directory)

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
pip install remote-avora

This installs the remote-avora command-line tool and its dependencies.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
remote-avora help

This prints the list of available commands.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
remote-avora installs the following Python package automatically:

Package Purpose fastapi[standard] Web framework and Uvicorn ASGI server

The [standard] extra includes Uvicorn, which is required to run the server, along with Pydantic and other common FastAPI dependencies.

docs.title: Development Installation
docs.text:
To install from source for development:

git clone https://github.com/Avora-Docx/Avora-Docx
cd legal-contract-version-control
pip install -e packages/remote_avora

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
To upgrade to the latest version:

pip install --upgrade remote-avora

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text: pip uninstall remote-avora

docs.title: Starting the Server
docs.text:
remote-avora serve

The server binds to all network interfaces (0.0.0.0) on port 8000. On startup it prints the local IP address so other users on your network can reach it.

Repositories are stored under ./repos/ in the current working directory. This directory is created automatically on first start.

docs.title: remote-avora serve
docs.text: Start the FastAPI server. Creates the repos/ directory if needed, prints the accessible URL, and starts Uvicorn.

docs.title: remote-avora help
docs.text: Print the list of available commands.

docs.title: HTTP Endpoints
docs.text: All endpoints are relative to the server base URL (e.g. http://<host>:8000).

docs.title: GET /
docs.text: Easter egg endpoint. Returns {"message": "Boo!"}.

docs.title: POST /repos/{repository_name}/publish
docs.text:
Publish a new repository. Accepts a multipart form with:

Field Description repository_name Name of the repository to create file A zip archive of the repository contents, named <repository_name>.zip data A JSON string containing {"remote": "<url>"} — the URL where the repository is hosted

The repository is extracted into a staging directory with zip-slip protection, then atomically moved into place. Returns {"message": "File published successfully", "repository_url": "<url>"}.

Limits: - Maximum 1000 files per zip - Maximum 100 MB total upload size - Maximum 10 MB per individual file

docs.title: GET /repos/{repository_name}/clone
docs.text: Download a repository as a zip archive. The response includes a Content-Disposition header for browser download.

docs.title: GET /repos/{repository_name}/push
docs.text: Returns the set of object identifiers currently stored in the remote repository. The local client uses this to determine which objects need to be uploaded.

docs.title: POST /repos/{repository_name}/push
docs.text:
Upload new objects to an existing repository. Accepts a zip archive named <repository_name>.zip containing only the changed objects. The archive is extracted into a staging copy of the repository, the metadata's updated_branches list is cleared, and the staging copy replaces the original atomically.

On failure the original repository is left untouched.

docs.title: POST /repos/{repository_name}/pull
docs.text:
Download missing objects and metadata. The request body is a JSON object:

{ "objects": ["<commit_hash>", ...] }

listing the object identifiers the local repository already has. The server responds with a zip archive containing only the objects the local is missing, plus the current metadata.json.

docs.title: Repository Name Validation
docs.text: Repository names must match the pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$ and cannot be . or ... This prevents path traversal and zip-slip attacks.

docs.title: Size and Count Limits
docs.text: Limit Value Max files per zip 1000 Max total upload size 100 MB Max individual file size 10 MB Constant Default Description REPOSITORIES_BASE_DIRECTORY ./repos Directory where repositories are stored NETWORK_IP 0.0.0.0 Bind address PORT_8000 8000 Listen port MAX_FILES_IN_ZIP 1000 Max files per zip archive MAX_TOTAL_UPLOAD_SIZE 100 MB Max total upload size MAX_INDIVIDUAL_FILE_SIZE 10 MB Max individual file size

docs.title: Client Configuration
docs.text:
On the client side, configure the remote URL with:

avora config remote http://<server-ip>:8000

The client automatically appends /repos/<repository-name>/ to construct full endpoint URLs.

docs.title: Workflow Example
docs.text:
# On the server host
remote-avora serve
# Server prints: Your Remote-Avora server will be accessible on your internet network at http://192.168.1.10:8000

# On the server host, publish a repository
avora init contract.docx
cd contract
avora config remote http://192.168.1.10:8000
avora publish

# On a client machine, clone the repository
avora clone http://192.168.1.10:8000/repos/contract/clone
cd contract

# Make changes and push
avora commit -m "Client edits"
avora push

# On the server host, pull changes
cd contract
avora pull

docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 2 Unexpected error
